Imagine a new employee who has just joined a company. On his very first week, he walks up to the CEO and says, "Your business strategy is frankly terrible, and I think you should listen to me instead." He has no experience, no authority, and no real standing to say something like that — yet he says it anyway, with complete boldness and zero respect.

That behavior — that specific kind of rudeness where someone speaks or acts in a way that goes far beyond what their position, age, or relationship allows — is impertinence.

Impertinence means rude, disrespectful, or shamelessly bold behavior or speech, especially from someone who has no right or standing to behave that way.

The word has two slightly different but related uses:

1. As an uncountable noun (a quality or state of behavior)

Here, impertinence refers to the general quality of being rude and disrespectful in that particular overstepping way. You use it to describe someone's manner or attitude as a whole.

  • "The impertinence of that young man shocked everyone in the room."
  • "She stared at him, stunned by his sheer impertinence."

In these sentences, impertinence is like a cloud hanging over someone's behavior — it describes the overall attitude, not a single moment.

2. As a countable noun (a specific rude act or remark)

Here, impertinence (or impertinences, in the plural) refers to a particular thing someone said or did that was rude and overstepping. Think of it as one concrete instance of that behavior.

  • "She had endured enough of his impertinences and decided to leave."
  • "What an impertinence — how dare he speak to her that way!"
The Special Flavor of This Word

This is important: impertinence is not just ordinary rudeness. If someone shouts at you in traffic, that's rude — but it's probably not called impertinence. The word carries a very specific flavor. It almost always involves:

  • A gap in status, age, experience, or authority — a student to a teacher, a child to a parent, a junior to a senior, a stranger asking something deeply personal.
  • Bold overstepping — the person does or says something they simply have no business saying or doing given who they are.
  • A lack of proper respect — not just careless rudeness, but an active failure to show the deference (respectful submission) that the situation calls for.

So the word quietly asks: "Who do you think you are to say/do that?" That underlying question is the soul of impertinence.

Impertinence can be used on a spectrum of severity.

On the more serious end, it describes genuinely offensive, disrespectful behavior that causes real offense:

  • "The reporter's impertinence — asking the grieving family such invasive questions — was widely condemned."

But it can also be used in a lighter, almost affectionate way, especially with children or in playful situations. A grandparent might laugh and say to a cheeky grandchild:

  • "Oh, the impertinence of this little one! Answering back at her age!"

Here the word is said with a raised eyebrow and a hidden smile. The child was cheeky and a little out of line — but it's charming rather than truly offensive.

So context and tone tell you whether impertinence is being used seriously or with a wink.
How It Feels to Be on the Receiving End

When someone experiences another person's impertinence, they usually feel a mix of:

  • Surprise — "Did they really just say/do that?"
  • Offense — a sense that their position, age, or dignity has not been respected.
  • Indignation — a feeling of "How dare they."

The word itself, when spoken aloud, often carries that indignant tone — "The impertinence!" said alone is a complete, expressive sentence that communicates all of those feelings at once.

Since you want a complete picture, here's how impertinence sits among related words — explained simply:

  • Rudeness is the broadest term. All impertinence is rude, but not all rudeness is impertinence. Rudeness is any unkind or discourteous behavior.
  • Impudence is very close to impertinence — shameless, disrespectful boldness. The difference is tiny: impudence leans slightly more toward shamelessness, while impertinence leans toward overstepping one's place.
  • Insolence is stronger and more contemptuous. An insolent person doesn't just overstep — they show open, deliberate contempt and defiance toward someone in authority. It has a harder, angrier edge.
  • Cheek (especially in British English) is the lightest version — cheeky behavior is mildly impertinent but usually said with some humor or fondness.

Think of it as a scale from mildest to strongest: cheek → impertinence / impudence → insolence.

Impertinence is rude, disrespectfully bold behavior or speech — especially from someone who has no standing, authority, or right to act that way given their position, age, or relationship to the other person. It carries a sense of "you have no business saying or doing that." It can be used to describe the overall quality of such behavior (uncountable) or a specific rude act or remark (countable). Depending on tone and context, it can describe something genuinely offensive or something merely cheeky and amusing.
